rv.q: There is no greater voice in modern musical theatre than McDonald and she lends those rich, glorious tones to both the title song and the original show's break-out hit (I'm Just) Wild About Harry.
"Shuffle Along" does all that historical stuff while putting on one helluva tap show.
“Shuffle Along” is, after “Hamilton,” the second best new musical of the Broadway year.
It is hard to imagine a better group than this one, finally, to tell the world about “Shuffle Along.”

Far from being an earnest history lesson, the new show is a crackling, high-energy tribute to the joys of creating entertainment — even at a time when black people weren’t allowed to display the full range of their talents.
Scene after scene dazzles in one of the most electrifying entertainments on Broadway.

This review might have begun 'Audra Smiles!' -- so unusual and uplifting is it to see our leading vocal tragedienne in a part that (until Act Two) is essentially as light as a soubrette's. McDonald sings beautifully, of course; the role sits mostly in the thrilling upper part of her range. But you may not have remembered...
It's not a review or revival. It's more like a history lesson that will blow you away.
Firsthand accounts suggest that the real Lottie Gee possessed those same traits.
Both the opening and closing numbers of this ebullient show pay homage to alumni of the original production of 'Shuffle Along' and those who followed.
The joy here is lessened by the lesson.
Shuffle Along, or The Making… struck me as both rough and unfinished...the show is conceptually flawed, and it's hard to tell whether that ever can be resolved.
Along is sometimes edifying and sometimes entertaining, but rarely do these twin aims coincide.
They have come up with a fascinating, colorfully grand entertainment.
In a year of pandering, corn-pone musicals, “Shuffle Along” exudes elegance and intelligence at every turn.
Clocking in at just shy of three hours, Shuffle Along never feels long — it’s a dazzling production that celebrates art, dreams, and equality.
It's important to remember that struggle — and exhilarating, when the tribute burns as brightly as this one.
This proudly flashy, impressively ambitious show is the very last production to open in the 2015-16 Broadway season.
Even though the narration lacks drama, the tap-happy new show gleams with ambition and topnotch talent.

“Shuffle Along” is moving, in fits and starts, as a story about artists who risk their critical and financial fortunes, sculpting a musical from their most raw emotional expressions and their sophisticated artistic heritage, instead of toning down that spirit for mass consumption.
Whether old or new, it is a hot mess of the highest caliber — a dazzling and dizzying documentary mixed with star turns, syncopated rhythms, stylish attire, fierce tap-dancing and weak subplots.

cn.t: A dazzling, electrifying spectacle with stellar performances and spectacular tap choreography, though critics note the show-within-a-show structure feels overstuffed and occasionally loses focus between entertainment and history lesson.

vs.sum: The Music Box Theatre offers excellent sightlines from most seats, making it ideal for intimate dramas, though sound quality can vary. The theater's charming Georgian-inspired design adds to its ambiance, while comfort and facilities are average for a Broadway venue.

acc.note: 5 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No steps from sidewalk. Infrared devices available.
